newsitem.title: USA: With handover, Hong Kong gains protector in U.S..
newsitem.headline: With handover, Hong Kong gains protector in U.S..

text.p: With the handover from British to Chinese control, Hong Kong was relieved of a colonial ruling power but gained a new international protector.
The way is now open for the United States to raise its voice more loudly than before on Hong Kong as the territory takes its place as the litmus test in U.S.-China ties.

New Beijing-Washington frictions are possible, even likely, over the former colony, although U.S. officials were impressed with the largely positive tone and content of the signals sent by China during the transition on June 30-July 1.
Ahead of the handover, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright laid down with increasing force and frequency markers for China's future treatment of Hong Kong.

"We expect officials both in Beijing and Hong Kong itself to respect the freedoms of the Hong Kong people; and we will be watching closely to see if free and fair elections for a new legislature are conducted as promised at an early date," she told one audience while in Hong Kong for the transition.

"It is essential ... that Hong Kong's open investment regime be maintained, its currency and customs and budget remain independent, its political life remain varied and free and its people allowed to go about their daily business under rules that were made not elsewhere but here in Hong Kong," Albright said.
The 1984 accord under which Hong Kong, now a special region under mainland communists, shed colonialism and set terms for its future was negotiated between Britain and China.
While acknowledging London's proprietary interest, Albright nevertheless asserted in a CNN interview: "We are the foremost world power and we have very important interests here."

Staking the U.S. claim, she noted that 36,000 Americans live in Hong Kong, more than the number of Britons, and it is the 13th largest U.S. trading partner. Some 1,100 American firms operate there, fuelling $24 billion in annual two-way trade and $14 billion in U.S. investment in the former colony.
Also, U.S. naval ships make 65 port calls a year; there is bilateral cooperation on drug trafficking and other crimes and a busy exchange of tourists and academics.
Washington, keen to improve U.S.-China ties before an October summit, is struggling to calibrate measured responses and not prejudge Beijing's handling of Hong Kong.

Albright hedged her bets on the appointed legislature China arranged to replace an elected body. She boycotted the new legislature's swearing-in. But affirming the need to deal with local Hong Kong and Chinese officials, she sent U.S. consul general Richard Boucher.

Also, Albright initially refrained from faulting China for sending 4,000 troops into Hong Kong the morning after the handover. A day later, with Britain denouncing Beijing, she branded the deployment "not ... the best way to start off."
Effecting the peaceful reintegration of Hong Kong, an economic power, was a proud achievement for China.
U.S. officials and other experts believe Beijing is aware of what's at stake -- money, improved U.S. ties and increased acceptance and clout in the international community.
President Jiang Zemin calmed some concerns when he vowed China would meet its commitments to Hong Kong, including on democracy. But plenty could go awry.

U.S. officials worry about provocations by rival Taiwan that could fan tensions with Beijing, Hong Kong activists who may push reforms too fast, as well as Hong Kong and Chinese leaders who interpret democracy too narrowly and do not agree that freedoms and an unfettered market are the key to success.

Also, the Chinese military could stray into prohibited political activity or tap profits from sales of U.S.-made technology that can be imported to Hong Kong under easier export rules than the mainland.
U.S. officials seem reasonably optimistic that over time, Hong Kong's freedoms, dynamism and lure of profits will force increased changes in China.

However, if concern for internal stability causes Beijing to put the brake on Hong Kong, the U.S. "ability to influence the outcome is mostly limited to diplomacy and public statements," said Morton Abramowitz, ex-president of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
